# Model from reference photos

When the person gives a few photos of one object from different sides (a side, the top, an end, a three-quarter view: product shots, phone photos, a drawing's views) and wants it in 3D, model a real solid from them, part by part, the way a designer does with Fusion's canvases or FreeCAD's image planes. Never answer with a relief (brightness made into height is a picture, not the object) or with one traced outline extruded flat: both look nothing like the object from any other side. Photogrammetry needs dozens of overlapping photos; a handful of separate views is this case.

1. **Read the photos first.** Name each one: which view it is (side, top, end, three-quarter), which way the object faces in it, whether it is taken square on and from far away (usable as a canvas) or at an angle (a three-quarter view: use it only to understand depth and how surfaces turn, never as a canvas). Write down every feature you see before modelling: the separate pieces and their materials and colours (a housing in two halves on a split line, a rubber grip, a cap, buttons, a trigger), openings and pockets, ribs, rails, vents, holes, lettering, and where the outline turns. That list is what you build; the silhouettes only give the outline.
2. **Ask for one real dimension** (overall length, height, a hole) unless the person gave one. If they cannot, estimate it from something of known size and make it a parameter, and say so. Every other size follows from the photos.
3. **Choose the axes**: the object's length along X, up +Z, the side view on the front plane. Place each usable view as a canvas on its plane, named for what it shows:

   ```
   ./ise canvas add attachments/side.jpg --name Side --plane front --object-width 165 --align "left bottom"
   ./ise canvas add attachments/end.jpg  --name End  --plane left  --object-height 133.9 --align "center bottom"
   ./ise canvas add attachments/top.jpg  --name Top  --plane top   --rotate -90 --object-width 165 --align "left middle"
   ```

   Planes are named by where the camera stands: `front` (from −Y; picture right is +X, up is +Z), `back` (from +Y: the object's other side, its right is −X), `left` (from −X, the end facing −X; picture right is −Y), `right` (from +X), `top` (from +Z; right +X, up +Y), `bottom`. With the length along X and the side photo showing the object's left side on `front`, the opposite side's photo goes on `back`, the end at −X on `left`. Turn a photo with `--rotate deg` (counter-clockwise) so its view reads the way the plane does; `--flip` mirrors it (only for a photo that really is mirrored). `--level u1,v1,u2,v2` turns a slightly tilted photo so a line that should be level is. An object that stood pitched or rolled for its photos (resting on a grip, a foot, a cable) is tilted in every view: in the side views that is a turn in the picture (`--level`), but in the end and top views the camera looked at it from a tilted direction, so pivot those canvases' planes by the same angle about the world axis it was pitched about (`--pivot y,-8.3`; check the sign by matching: the wrong way doubles the error). Match reports compare along the canvas's own (pivoted) direction.

   Size and register them by the object itself: `--object-width` / `--object-height` / `--object WxH` set the scale from the object's outline (what stands out from the backdrop) and `--align` puts a corner or middle of its bounds at the plane's origin, so every view shares one origin (here the front end at x = 0, the bottom at z = 0, the centre line at y = 0). Stand the object on z = 0, as it rests (bottom down): the view's ground is at z = 0, and a model built below it shows through the floor. Name sides from the object's own point of view: its left side is the one on your left when it points away from you, so a side photo with the object's front on the picture's left shows its left side. Chain them: size the side by the real length, read the height it reports (`object: 165 × 133.9 mm`), size the end view by that height, then check the widths agree between top and end (within 2–3 %). When they disagree, the photo is not square on: crop to the part that is (`--crop l,t,r,b` pixels), stretch a foreshortened one (`--object LxW`), or square it up from four corners of a rectangle on the object and its true size (`--perspective u1,v1,u2,v2,u3,v3,u4,v4,WxH`, corners top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left). `--calibrate u1,v1,u2,v2,mm` (two pixels a known distance apart), `--width` and `--scale` size it by other means; `--at x,y,z` moves the plane (the anchor pixel lands there; `--anchor u,v` picks it). A busy or coloured backdrop: `--background r,g,b` and `--threshold`. `./ise canvas list` shows them; `canvas update <name> …` changes one (the person sees them in the view, can hide them, and calibrates by picking two points).
4. **Read sizes from the photos in millimetres.** `./ise canvas measure Side --every 5` prints the outline's bounds and area and, every 5 mm across and up, where it runs (its spans); add `--channel brightness --threshold 0.35` for only what is dark (a black grip), `--region l,t,r,b` for one area of the photo in pixels. In a program:

   ```js
   const side = canvas("Side");
   side.silhouette()                               // the whole object's outline (Profile) on the plane, in mm
   side.trace({ channel: "brightness", threshold: 0.35, largest: true })   // only what is dark: the black grip, a trigger
   side.trace({ channel: "brightness", region: [u0, v0, u1, v1] })         // only inside a box of pixels
   side.spans({ x: 120 })                          // where the outline is at x = 120: [[zBottom, zTop], …]
   side.toPlane([u, v]); side.toWorld([u, v])      // a pixel you read on the photo, in mm (plane / world)
   ```

   Separate pieces by colour this way (a black grip on a yellow body); measure a feature's place and size from its pixels (open the photo, read where it is) or its own trace; `metric(…)` the numbers you measured, so they show.
5. **Start from the views, then build the real object.** `fromViews([canvas("Side"), canvas("Top"), canvas("End")])` intersects the views' outlines pushed through the model (the visual hull): the right outline from every side, but square in section and solid inside. It is the starting block and a trimming tool, not the part. Then, part by part:
   - Each separately made piece is its own `part(…)` with its material (yellow housing halves, black rubber grip, black trigger and switch, a yellow butt plate…); hull each from its own colour's trace, or cut the hull where the photos show the joint.
   - Give the sections their real shape. `loftViews([side, end], { along: "z", roundness: 2.5, profiles: { Side: grip } })` stacks rounded sections (superellipses: roundness 2 an ellipse, 4 a soft box, 8 nearly square) whose width comes from one view and depth from the other at every station, so a grip, handle or nose is round in section and still follows both outlines (finger grooves, tapers) exactly; use it for every organic piece. For boxy pieces, intersect `fromViews` with a box whose long edges are rounded, or loft through sections drawn from the end view. Trim with the side outline (`side.extrude(200, { from: -100, profile })`, then `intersect`) to keep the profile exactly on the photo. Traced outlines have hundreds of short edges: `fillet` and `shell` on them fail; round them with `loftViews`, with `profile.offset(-r).offset(r)` (rounds a profile's corners before extruding), or by building that piece from primitives at the measured sizes. Keep a program built on traced outlines on the fast mesh kernel: a single `fillet`, `chamfer`, `shell`, `draft`, `loft`, `sweep` or solid `offset` anywhere in it sends the whole program to the exact kernel, which takes minutes on traced outlines; round small pieces in 2D (rounded profiles) instead, or make a piece that needs true fillets its own shape.
   - Cut what is open: bays, pockets and hollows (subtract the opening's outline, traced from the end view where it shows a different colour or shade, or the body's own section offset inward by the wall, as deep as the side view shows; `shell` only on bodies built from primitives), the trigger guard's opening, holes.
   - Add what stands proud or is cut in: rails and ridges (a pattern of blocks or cuts at the pitch you measure), sight towers and their holes, vents and slots, buttons and switches, grip grooves, lettering only if it is moulded.
   - A housing made in two halves is two parts split on its centre plane (each half the body intersected with a half-space), with the split line showing.
6. **Compare every view and iterate until it matches**: `./ise canvas match all` draws the model square to each canvas over its photo and reports the silhouette overlap (IoU, 1 is perfect), how far the outlines are apart (mean and worst mm) and each region of extra (red) or missing (blue) material, with where it is in mm. Read the overlay pictures (`look/match-*.png`), fix the largest differences first, and run it again. Aim for IoU ≥ 0.9 on the side view and ≥ 0.85 on the others (oblique or perspective-heavy photos score lower: say why). The outline is not the whole check: look at the model from iso and three-quarter views (`./ise look --view 35,25`) beside the three-quarter photos, since sections, depths and details only show there. Keep the main view's match as a requirement: `intent.requirement.create { rule: { kind: "silhouette_match", part, canvas, min_iou: 0.9 } }` (optionally `max_deviation: { value: 2, unit: "mm" }`), re-checked on every change.
7. **Report** the views used, how the scale was set (the dimension given, or estimated), the IoU per view, the parts and their materials, and what had to be judged rather than seen (wall thickness, hidden insides, the far side). Leave the canvases in the project (hidden if they are in the way: `canvas update Side --hide`); they are reference, never exported, never in the BOM.
